The 3 questions that distinguish the systems

The most reliable way to distinguish British land revenue settlements is to identify who was responsible for the government's demand, how the amount was assessed and whether it could be revised.

The settlement also affected the relationship between those who cultivated the land and those who exercised rights over it.

Comparison of the principal features

FeaturePermanent SettlementRyotwari SettlementMahalwari Settlement
Principal introduction1793Late 18th and early 19th centuries1822
Associated officialsLord CornwallisAlexander Read and Thomas MunroHolt Mackenzie
Main settlement unitZamindari estateIndividual cultivator's holdingMahal or village revenue estate
Principal revenue payerZamindarIndividual ryotVillage estate through recognised representatives
Role of intermediariesZamindar collected rent and paid revenueNo zamindar required as principal revenue intermediaryVillage headman or recognised representatives arranged collection
Landholding rightsEstate-level zamindari rights strengthened; tenant rights variedIndividual cultivator recognised as holder, subject to applicable conditionsVillage and co-sharer rights recognised; individual rights also recorded
Government revenue demandFixed in perpetuityPeriodically revisablePeriodically revisable
Principal regionsBengal and BiharMadras and Bombay PresidenciesNorth-Western Provinces and parts of Punjab
Major difficultiesHigh rent, tenant insecurity and estate auctionsHeavy assessments, debt and pressure from officialsHigh assessments and pressure on village communities

How rights and incentives differed

Permanent Settlement

The zamindar was responsible for a fixed government demand. If cultivation and rents increased, the zamindar could retain additional income after paying the government's revenue demand.

This provided a possible incentive to improve agriculture. However, a high initial assessment, the risk of losing the estate and opportunities to earn rent without investment often weakened that incentive.

For cultivators, the settlement did not itself establish permanently fixed rents or equal tenancy protection.

Ryotwari Settlement

The individual cultivator became directly responsible for government revenue and generally held recognised rights over the assessed holding.

The absence of the zamindar as the principal revenue payer could strengthen the direct relationship between cultivator and state. Nevertheless, high assessments and the threat of revenue enforcement could make cultivation financially difficult.

Because assessments were revisable, the government could reconsider its demand rather than remaining bound by a permanently fixed amount.

Mahalwari Settlement

The village or revenue estate formed the main assessment unit, while recognised village representatives arranged revenue collection.

The system preserved an important administrative role for village institutions. However, the responsibility for satisfying the demand could place pressure on the community and increase the influence of powerful headmen or co-sharers.

Like Ryotwari, it allowed periodic revision of the government's assessment.

Understanding the consequences of different revenue arrangements

The burden of a poor harvest or a decline in crop prices could appear differently under each settlement.

  • Permanent Settlement: A zamindar remained responsible for the fixed government demand even when tenants struggled to pay rent. Failure to meet the demand could lead to an estate auction.
  • Ryotwari: The individual cultivator directly faced the government's assessed demand. An inability to pay could lead to borrowing, arrears and enforcement action.
  • Mahalwari: Difficulties experienced by cultivators affected the revenue-paying capacity of the mahal. The village headman and recognised co-sharers could face pressure to meet the estate-level obligation.

These were possible outcomes of the revenue arrangements, not identical consequences in every district or every agricultural season.

Important distinctions in statement-based reasoning

Permanent revenue did not mean permanent tenancy

The government's demand on a zamindari was permanently fixed, but the settlement did not automatically provide permanent occupancy rights or fixed rents to all cultivators.

Direct settlement did not eliminate every intermediary

Ryotwari removed the zamindar from the main government revenue relationship. It did not eliminate revenue officials, moneylenders, private landlords or other influential persons who might affect cultivators.

Surveying individual fields did not make Mahalwari identical to Ryotwari

Both systems could involve the measurement and assessment of individual plots. Their principal distinction was that Ryotwari assessed the individual ryot as the revenue payer, whereas Mahalwari organised the government demand around the revenue estate.

Periodically revised revenue was not necessarily low revenue

Both Ryotwari and Mahalwari allowed later revisions. This did not guarantee moderate assessments. Officials could impose demands that cultivators considered excessive.

Village-based responsibility did not imply equal land ownership

The Mahalwari system recognised village-level institutions and, in many cases, joint responsibility. Individual families and co-sharers could still hold different rights and exercise unequal influence within the village.

A regional association was not an exclusive territorial rule

Permanent Settlement is strongly associated with Bengal, Ryotwari with Madras and Bombay, and Mahalwari with the North-Western Provinces. However, different arrangements and local exceptions existed within colonial territories.

Final understanding

The 3 principal British land revenue systems represented different methods of organising the relationship between government, landholders, village institutions and cultivators.

Permanent Settlement relied primarily on zamindars and fixed the government's demand permanently. Ryotwari made individual cultivators directly responsible for revenue. Mahalwari treated the village or revenue estate as the principal settlement unit.

Ryotwari and Mahalwari allowed periodic reassessment, whereas Permanent Settlement did not.

Despite their differences, all 3 operated within a colonial administration that placed substantial importance on obtaining agricultural revenue. High assessments, unequal landholding rights and difficulties of payment often contributed to rural indebtedness and insecurity.

Prelims focus

  • Cornwallis, 1793: Permanent Settlement with zamindars and a permanently fixed government demand.
  • Alexander Read and Thomas Munro: Associated with Ryotwari and direct settlement with cultivators.
  • Holt Mackenzie, 1822: Mahalwari Settlement in the North-Western Provinces.
  • Permanent versus revisable: Permanent Settlement fixed the government's demand in perpetuity; Ryotwari and Mahalwari generally allowed periodic revision.
  • Individual versus village: Ryotwari assessed the individual cultivator; Mahalwari assessed the mahal as the revenue estate.
  • Trap: The absence of zamindars as principal revenue intermediaries did not automatically ensure secure, prosperous or debt-free cultivators.
